column2: Fierce winds blew and the ocean was agitated; the fires did not blaze and the sun did not shine.
The planets did not shine, nor the constellations nor the stars; the sages did not shine, nor the gods, nor the Danavas.
When all had thus become dark, the lords of the hosts burned everything; others broke the sacrificial posts and tore them up terribly.
Some roared, others made strange forms, and others ran swiftly, fast as the wind and quick as thought.
The sacrificial vessels and the halls of sacrifice were smashed; being shattered, they looked like stars falling from the sky.
There were heaps of divine food, drink and eatables like mountains, rivers of milk, and others with mud of ghee and milk-rice,
divine rivers with water of honey-cream, with sands of candied sugar, others carrying the six tastes, and lovely streams of molasses.
Meats of every kind, various eatables, and whatever divine things there were to lick and suck,
the fierce ones born of Rudra's wrath, like the fire of doom, devoured with their various mouths, plundered and threw about.
Devouring, huge as mountains, terrifying everyone on all sides, those of various shapes sported and carried off the women of the gods.
Thus the valiant Virabhadra, joined with those hosts and impelled by Rudra's wrath, the sacrifice that had been well protected by all the gods —
he quickly burned that sacrifice in the presence of Bhadrakali; others raised cries terrifying to all beings.
Others cut off the head of the Sacrifice and roared terribly. Then the gods led by Shakra, and Daksha the lord of creatures, joined their palms and said, "Tell us, who are you?"

I am not a god nor a Daitya, nor have I come here to eat, nor to see, O lords of gods, nor out of curiosity.
brahmapuran:39:71	I have come to destroy Daksha's sacrifice, O best of gods. I am known as Virabhadra, born from the wrath of Rudra.
brahmapuran:39:72	And this is the famous Bhadrakali, who came forth from the Goddess's anger; sent by the god of gods, she has come to the sacrifice.
brahmapuran:39:73	O king of kings, take refuge in the god of gods, the husband of Uma; even the god's anger is better than a boon from his attendants.
With sacrificial posts dug up and torn out and thrown here and there, with vultures greedy for flesh flying up and swooping down,
scattered by the wind of their wings, resounding with the howls of jackals, that king's sacrifice, oppressed then by the hosts,
took the form of a deer and flew up into the sky. Perceiving that sacrifice going away in that form,
the Lord took up his bow and arrow and went after it. Then from the forehead of that lord of hosts, of boundless splendour, in his anger,
a terrible drop of sweat flowed out. As soon as that drop of sweat fell on the ground,
a great fire appeared, like the blazing fire of doom; and from it, O best of brahmins, arose a person —
short, yet huge, red-eyed, green-bearded, terrifying, with hair standing up, very hairy, with red ears,
dreadful and dark in colour, wearing red garments. That mighty one burned that sacrifice as fire burns dry grass.
All the gods fled in fear to the ten directions. As he moved about there with his might,
the whole earth with its seven continents shook on every side. When that great being, terrifying to the world of the gods, had arisen,
then I, worshipping Mahadeva, said to him: "O Lord, all the gods will give you a share.
Let this be withdrawn by you, O lord of all gods. All these deities and thousands of sages
have found no peace because of your anger, Mahadeva. And this person born of your sweat, O bull among gods,
named Fever, O knower of dharma, will roam the worlds. The whole earth cannot bear his concentrated splendour, O Lord;
let him be divided in many ways." Thus addressed by me, and a share having been assigned to him,
the Lord, the god of gods bearing Pinaka, said to me, "So be it," and the bearer of Pinaka himself was greatly pleased.
Daksha too took refuge in his mind in the god Bhava. Restraining his in-breath and out-breath with effort at the place of the eyes,
holding his gaze in all directions, the many-eyed conqueror of foes smiled and said, "Tell me, what shall I do for you?"
When the great account had been recited to the gods and the ancestors, Daksha, the lord of creatures, afraid and anxious, his face and eyes tearful, joined his palms and said to the god:

If the Lord is pleased, if I am dear to you, if I am worthy of favour, and if a boon is to be given me —
brahmapuran:39:94	whatever of the sacrificial materials has been eaten, drunk, scattered, destroyed, crushed and thrown away,
brahmapuran:39:95	gathered over a long time and with great effort — let it not be in vain for me, by your grace, O Maheshvara.
So be it, said the Lord Hara, who took away Bhaga's eyes. And the lord of creatures, to Mahadeva, the three-eyed overseer of dharma,
kneeling on the ground, having obtained the boon from Bhava, Daksha praised the bull-bannered god with a thousand and eight names.
To the one of various distorted faces, with a tongue like a sword and fierce fangs, whose portions are fortnights, months and moments, who loves the gourd-lute;
to the one of forms both gentle and terrible, more terrible than the terrible; salutation to Shiva, the tranquil; salutation to the most tranquil;
salutation to the awakened, the pure, who loves sharing; to the wind, to the bird; salutation to the one devoted to Sankhya;
salutation to the one with a single fierce bell, who speaks with bells, who bears a bell, who has a hundred thousand bells, who loves garlands of bells;
to the staff of life, the eternal; salutation to you, the red one; to Rudra who utters "hum hum," who loves the form of the yoni;
salutation ever to the boundless, who loves mountains and trees; salutation to the lord of sacrifice, to the being, to the one who is born;
to the bearer of sacrifice, the self-controlled, the one to be worshipped with austerity, and to Bhaga; salutation to the bank, to the one of the bank, salutation to the lord of rivers;
to the giver of food, the lord of food; salutation to the eater of food; salutation to the thousand-headed, the thousand-footed,
the one with a thousand raised tridents, the thousand-eyed; salutation to the one coloured like the morning sun, who bears the form of a child,
salutation to the one in the form of the morning sun, who plays like a child; salutation to the pure, the awakened, the agitator and destroyer,
whose hair is marked with waves, salutation to the one with loosened hair; salutation to the one devoted to the six duties and bound by the three duties,
who duly establishes the separate dharmas of the classes and stages of life; salutation to the best, the eldest; salutation to the tumultuous,
with white and tawny eyes, with black and red eyes; to dharma, desire, wealth and liberation; to the slayer and the destroyer;
to Sankhya, the chief of Sankhya, the lord of yoga, salutation; salutation to the lord of streets and highways, to the path of the crossroads;
with a black antelope skin as upper garment and a serpent as sacred thread; O Ishana, host of Rudras, Harikesha, salutation to you!
O three-eyed one, lord of Ambika, manifest and unmanifest, salutation to you; O Kala, giver of desires and destroyer of desire, slayer of the wicked and unruly,
censured by all, destroyer of all, Sadyojata, salutation to you; O maddener, whose hair is wet with the water of the hundred-whirled Ganga,
whirl joined with the crescent moon, whirl of clouds, salutation to you; salutation to the maker of gifts of food, salutation to the source of food-givers;
you are the eater of food and the protector, and the fire of dissolution. The womb-born, the egg-born, the sweat-born and the sprout-born —
you alone, lord of the gods, are the fourfold host of beings; you are the creator of the moving and unmoving, and you alone are the withdrawer.
You alone are Brahma, lord of the universe; they call you Brahman in the waters; you are the supreme source of all, the nectar-rayed one, the treasury of lights.
The expounders of Brahman call you the Rik and Saman and the syllable Om; "haayi haayi hare haayi huvaahaava" —
so the best of gods, the Saman-singers and expounders of Brahman, sing to you; you consist of the Yajus and the Rik, joined with the Saman and the Atharvan;
you are recited by the knowers of Brahman with the ranks of the Kalpas and Upanishads. The brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas, shudras and the classes and stages of life —
you alone are the assemblies of the stages of life, the lightning and the thunder; you are the year, the seasons, the months and the half-months,
kala, kashtha, the blink of the eye, the constellations and the ages; you are the hump of bulls and the peaks of mountains,
the lion among beasts, Takshaka and Ananta among serpents, the milk ocean among oceans and the pranava among mantras,
the thunderbolt among weapons and truth among vows; you alone are desire and hatred, passion, delusion, calm and forbearance,
resolution, steadfastness, greed, desire and anger, victory and defeat; you bear the mace, the arrow, the bow, the khatvanga and the mallet;
you are the cutter, the piercer, the striker, the leader and the thinker, in our view; dharma with its ten marks, wealth and desire,
the moon, the ocean, rivers, ponds and lakes, creepers, vines, grasses and herbs, cattle, beasts and birds,
the beginning of substance, action and quality, the giver of flowers and fruits in season, the beginning, end and middle, the Gayatri and the syllable Om;
green, red, black, blue and yellow, the moment, tawny, brown, dove-coloured and the macchaka;
famed as having golden seed, considered golden, named golden and fond of gold;
you are Indra and Yama, Varuna, the giver of wealth and fire; the blooming one, the bright-rayed, Svarbhanu and the sun;
the office of hotri, the hotri, the oblation and what is offered, the Lord; the Trisauparna, O Brahman, and the Shatarudriya of the Yajus;
the purifier of purifiers, the auspiciousness of auspicious things; you are life and you are rajas, tamas joined with sattva;
prana, apana, samana, udana and vyana, the opening and closing of the eyes, hunger, thirst and yawning;
red-limbed, fanged, great-mouthed, great-bellied, with pure hair, green beard, upstanding hair, moving and unmoving;
whose limbs are song, instrument and dance, fond of song and music; the fish, the net, the water, the invincible, the water-serpent, the hut-dweller;
the untimely, the good time, the bad time, the destroyer of time; death, the imperishable, the end, the maker of forbearance and illusion;
Samvarta and Vartaka, the Samvartaka and the cloud; the one with bells, the bell-bearer, the crested one, the salt ocean;
Brahma, with a mouth like the fire of doom, the staff-bearer, the shaven one, bearing the triple staff; of four ages, four Vedas, four priests and four paths;
leader of the four stages of life and maker of the four classes; perishable and imperishable, beloved, rogue, counted by hosts, lord of hosts;
wearing red garlands and garments, lord of the mountain, beloved of the mountain's daughter, lord of artisans, best of artisans, originator of all crafts;
ender of Bhaga's eyes, the fierce, destroyer of Pushan's teeth; Svaha, Svadha, the Vashat call and the salutation — salutation to you!
Of hidden vows, hidden, served by those of hidden vows; the crosser, the one who carries across, the saviour among all beings;
the establisher, the ordainer, the joiner, the depositor, the upholder, the bearer; austerity, Brahman, truth, celibacy and uprightness;
self of beings, maker of beings, being, the source of past, future and present; Bhur, Bhuvar and Svar; being, fire, Maheshvara;
Brahmavarta, Suravarta, Kamavarta — salutation to you; destroyer of Kama's form, fond of garlands of karnikara flowers;
leader of cattle, the one who moves among cattle, whose mount is the lord of bulls; protector of the three worlds, Govinda, protector, Gogarga;
facing the full moon, fair-faced, fierce-faced, faceless, four-faced, many-faced, ever facing the foe in battle;
Hiranyagarbha, the bird, the giver of wealth, the lord of wealth, Viraj; slayer of adharma, the great Daksha, bearer of the staff, fond of battle;
standing, steady, the pillar, unshaking and very firm; hard to ward off, hard to bear, unbearable, hard to overcome;
hard to hold, hard to control, eternal, hard to humble, victory and conqueror; the hare, the moon-eyed, cold and heat, hunger, thirst and old age;
mental and bodily ailments, the destroyer and lord of disease; the bearable, the hunter of the sacrificial deer, the mine of diseases and not their mine;
crested, the lotus, lotus-eyed; bearer of the staff and discus-staff, destroyer of the fierce share;
drinker of poison and of nectar, drinker of wine, of milk and Soma; drinker of honey and of water, drinker of all, strong and weak;
with limbs of the bull, the bull, bull-eyed, famed as the bull, honoured by the worlds;
the moon and sun are your eyes and the Grandsire your heart; the Agnishtoma is your body, adorned by dharma and ritual.
Neither Brahma, nor Govinda, nor the ancient sages can truly know your greatness, O Shiva.
May your auspicious, subtle forms come into my sight; protect me with them on all sides, as a father protects his own son.
Protect me — I am to be protected by you, O sinless one; salutation to you. You are the Lord compassionate to devotees, and I am ever devoted to you.
He who, covering many thousands of men hard to see, stands alone at the ocean's end — may he always be my protector.
To him whom yogins, sleepless, breath controlled, established in sattva, seeing all equally, behold as light, to him whose self is yoga, salutation.
I take refuge in the one who lies on the waters, who, having devoured all beings when the end of the age comes, sleeps in the midst of the waters.
He who, entering the mouth of Rahu, drinks the moon at night and, becoming Svarbhanu, swallows the sun, and is the fire of Soma —
may those thumb-sized persons who dwell in the bodies of all embodied beings always protect me and always nourish me.
Those by whom embryos are produced and the waters that have their share — through them Svaha and Svadha reach and are relished.
Those by whom living beings in the body grow and weep, rejoice and are not drawn away — salutation to them always.
Those in the ocean, in river fastnesses, on mountains and in caves, at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, in wildernesses and thickets,
at crossroads, in streets, in squares and in assembly halls, in stables of elephants, horses and chariots, in old gardens and houses,
in the five elements, in the directions and intermediate directions, those between Indra and the sun, and those in the rays of the moon and sun,
those who have gone to Rasatala and those who have gone beyond it — salutation to them, salutation to them, salutation to them in every way.
You are all, the all-pervading god, Bhava, lord of all beings, the inner self of all beings; that is why you were not invited.
You alone are worshipped, O god, with sacrifices of various fees; you alone are the maker of all; that is why you were not invited.
Or else, O god, I was deluded by your subtle maya; for that reason too you were not invited by me.
Be gracious to me, O lord of the gods; you alone are my refuge; you are my goal and my foundation, and there is no other — this is my conviction.
Having praised Mahadeva thus, the great-minded one fell silent; and the Lord, well pleased, spoke again to Daksha:
I am well satisfied with you, Daksha, by this hymn, O one of good vows; what need to say more? You will come near me.
Then Bhava, lord of the three worlds, the omniscient, spoke these reassuring words:

Daksha, do not grieve over the destruction of the sacrifice. I am the destroyer of sacrifice for you; this was seen long ago, O sinless one.
brahmapuran:40:105	Take from me this further boon, O one of good vows; be glad and pleasant of face, and listen to me with a concentrated mind.
brahmapuran:40:106	By my grace, O lord of creatures, you will share in the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices and a hundred Vajapeya sacrifices.
brahmapuran:40:107	Understand the Vedas with their six limbs and Sankhya and Yoga completely, and practise vast austerity, hard even for gods and Danavas.
brahmapuran:40:108	Joined with twelve years, secret, blamed by the ignorant, practised in some places according to the dharmas of classes and stages of life and not in others,
brahmapuran:40:109	agreed upon and resolved, freeing creatures from their fetters, the Pashupata vow, for all the stages of life,
brahmapuran:40:110	has been produced by me, Daksha — auspicious and releasing from all sins. Whatever abundant fruit comes from its proper observance, may that be yours, O illustrious one; let the fever of your mind be cast off.
Having said this, the lord of the gods, with his wife and followers, vanished from the sight of Daksha of boundless splendour.
Having obtained his share as Uma had said, Bhava, knower of all dharma, then divided the fever in many ways
for the peace of all beings — hear now, O twice-born: heat of the head for elephants, bitumen for mountains,
know it as moss for waters, the sloughed skin for serpents, foot-disease for cattle, and salinity on the earth's surface;
for dogs, O knowers of dharma, the obstruction of sight; for horses, the disease of the nostrils; for peacocks, the bursting of the crest;
redness of eyes for cuckoos; for the great souls it is declared to be hatred; for all people, dissension — so we have heard;
for all parrots the fever is said to be hiccup; for tigers, O brahmins, fever here is called exhaustion;
and among humans, O all-knowing ones, it is called fever; it is placed at death, at birth and in between.
This is Maheshvara's very terrible splendour called fever; the Lord is to be saluted and honoured by all living beings.
The man who, with an undismayed mind and well composed, always reads this origin of fever, becomes free from disease, joyful, and obtains his desires as he wishes.
Whoever recites or hears the hymn spoken by Daksha meets with no misfortune and obtains long life.
As the Lord Bhava is foremost among all the gods, so this hymn composed by Daksha is foremost among hymns.
It should be recited with devotion and care by those who desire fame, heaven, divine lordship, wealth and victory, and by those who desire knowledge.
A man who is ill, sorrowful, wretched, seized by fear and the like, or engaged in the king's service, is freed from great fear.
In this very body he obtains happiness in this world from Maheshvara and becomes a king of the hosts.
Neither Yakshas nor Pishachas, nor Nagas nor Vinayakas can cause obstacles in the house where Bhava is praised.
A woman devoted to Bhava who hears this with devotion becomes honoured in her father's family and in her husband's.
Whoever hears all this or recites it often — all his undertakings succeed without obstacle.
Whatever is thought in the mind and whatever is spoken in words — all is accomplished for him by the recitation of this hymn.
Having made an offering, divided for the god with Guha, the Goddess and Nandishvara, with self-restraint and discipline,
thereafter, engaged, he should quickly take up the names in due order; the man obtains the wealth, desires and enjoyments he seeks.
When he dies he attains heaven, surrounded by a thousand women; whether endowed with all desires or burdened with all sins,
reciting the hymn made by Daksha he is freed from all sins; and when he dies, honoured by gods and Asuras, he attains union with the hosts.
He shines in a celestial car yoked with a bull, and becomes a follower of Rudra until the dissolution of beings.
So said the Lord Vyasa, son of Parashara. No one knows this, and it should not be recited to just anyone.
Having heard this supreme secret, even those of sinful birth — vaishyas, women and shudras — would attain the world of Rudra.
A twice-born who always recites it to brahmins on every festival day attains the world of Rudra; there is no doubt.
crowded with houses and gate-towers, adorned with gates at the three-way junctions, full of various merchants and beautiful with various gems,
with city towers, adorned with charioteers and beautiful with white mansions like royal swans,
with roads and gates, beautiful with white ramparts, protected by bands of armed men and adorned with moats,
adorned with banners of white, red, yellow, black and dark hues tossed by the wind,
delighted with constant festivals, with the sounds of various instruments, adorned with lutes, flutes, drums and catapults,
adorned everywhere with divine temples set with ramparts and gardens and with variously arranged worship.
Joyful women are seen there, slender-waisted, their necks adorned with necklaces, their eyes long as lotus petals,
with full, raised breasts, youthful, with faces like the full moon, with steady locks and fine cheeks, sounding with girdles and anklets,
with lovely hair and fine hips, eyes reaching to their ears, endowed with every good mark and adorned with every ornament,
wearing divine garments, fair, some like gold, walking like swans and elephants, bent with the weight of their breasts,
their limbs anointed with divine perfumes, adorned with ear-ornaments, languid with intoxication, with lovely hips and ever-smiling faces,
their teeth slightly showing, lips like bimba fruit, sweet-voiced, their mouths reddened with betel, clever and pleasing to see,
fortunate, sweet-spoken, ever proud of their youth, all wearing divine garments and always adorned with good conduct.
Those women, like Apsarases, always sport there, joyful in their own homes day and night, with lovely faces.
Men are seen there, proud of beauty and youth, endowed with every good mark, with polished jewelled earrings.
Brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, O best of sages, very righteous and devoted to their own dharma, dwell there.
Other chief courtesans dwell there too, with lovely eyes, equal to Ghritachi and Menaka and equal to Tilottama,
like Urvashi and like Viprachitti, resembling Vishvachi and Sahajanya, and like Pramlocha.
All of them are sweet-spoken and all smiling, all skilled in the arts and all endowed with virtues.
Thus courtesans skilled in dance and song dwell there, O best of sages, proud of all feminine accomplishments,
skilled in glances and conversation, beautiful and pleasing to see — not lacking beauty, not of bad conduct, not doing harm to others,
at the fall of whose sidelong glances men are bewitched. There are no poor there, no fools, no haters of others,
no sick, no unclean, no misers, no deceivers, none lacking beauty, none of bad conduct, none who harm others.
Such men dwell in that region famed in the world, where movement is pleasant everywhere and brings happiness to all beings,
crowded with various peoples and rich in all crops, with karnikaras, jackfruits, champakas and nagakesaras,
patalas, ashokas, bakulas, many kapitthas and dhavas, mangoes, nimbas and kadambas, and other kinds of flowers,
shining with nipas, dhavas, khadiras and creepers, with shalas, palmyras, tamalas, coconuts and shubhanjanas,
with arjunas, saptaparnas, kovidaras and pippalas, lakuchas, saralas, lodhras, hintalas and devadarus,
with palashas, muchukundas, parijatas and kubjakas, groves of plantains, jambus and areca palms,
with ketakis, karaviras, atimuktas and kimshukas, mandara and kunda flowers, and other kinds of flowers,
with gardens like Nandana, pleasant with the cries of various birds, with trees bent under loads of fruit and masses of flowers of every season,
with chakoras, shatapatras, bhringarajas and cuckoos, sparrows, peacocks, priyaputras and parrots,
jivanjivakas, haritas and chatakas dwelling in the woods, and other flocks of birds singing with sweet voices,
with long ponds, tanks, lotus pools and step-wells, and other various reservoirs adorned with clusters of lotuses,
with water-lilies, white lotuses and lovely blue lotuses, with kadambas, chakravakas and water-fowl,
karandavas, plavas, swans and other water-birds. Thus with trees of various kinds and excellent flowers of various kinds,
and with various holy reservoirs, it is beautiful all around. There dwells the god himself, clad in hide, bull-bannered,
Shiva, giver of enjoyment and liberation, for the good of all the world. The holy places on earth, the rivers and lakes,
lotus pools, tanks, wells, springs and seas — having first gathered drops of water from each of them separately,
for the good of all the worlds, Rudra, with all the gods, made in that region, O best of brahmins, a holy place named Bindusaras,
together with the sages; therefore it is remembered as Bindusaras. On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Margashirsha, O best of brahmins,
whoever makes a pilgrimage there at the equinox, with senses controlled, bathing duly in Bindusaras with faith,
and, silent, satisfies the gods, sages, men and ancestors with sesame water according to rule, knowing the procedure of names and lineages,
having bathed there duly, obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. At an eclipse, the equinox, the solar transit and the solstice,
at the beginnings of the ages, at the shadashiti and on other auspicious days, those who give wealth and the like to brahmins there
obtain a hundredfold the fruit of other holy places. Those who offer rice-balls to the ancestors on the bank of the lake
bring imperishable satisfaction to the ancestors, without doubt. Then, going to Shambhu's temple, silent and with senses controlled,
entering, one should worship Sharva after circumambulating him three times; having bathed Bhava with ghee, milk and the like, being pure,
anointing him with fragrant sandal and saffron, one should then worship the god, the moon-crested husband of Uma,
with various pure flowers — bilva, arka, lotus and others — worshipping Shankara with the mantra stated in the Agamas and that stated in the Veda.
One who is not initiated should worship with the name alone and with the root mantra. Having worshipped the god thus with perfumes and flowers he loves,
with incense, lamps, food offerings, presents and hymns, with prostrations like a staff and with charming songs and music,
with dances, recitations, salutations, cries of victory and circumambulations — having worshipped the god of gods, the husband of Uma, duly in this way,
freed from all sins, proud of beauty and youth, having raised twenty-one generations of his family, adorned with divine ornaments,
in a golden celestial car hung with networks of bells, sung to by Gandharvas and adorned with Apsarases,
illuminating all the directions, he goes to Shiva's world. Having enjoyed there, O brahmins, happiness that delights the mind,
with the dwellers of that world until the dissolution of beings, he then comes back here to earth when his merit is exhausted,
and is born in the house of yogins, a knower of the four Vedas, O best of brahmins; having attained the Pashupata yoga, he then attains liberation.
At the god's lying down and rising, at the solar transit and solstice, on the Ashoka eighth and at the Pavitraropana festival,
those who see that supreme god clad in hide go to Shiva's world in a celestial car coloured like the sun.
The wise who see that god at any time are also freed from sin and go to Shiva's world.
To the west, east, south and north of the god, for two and a half yojanas, is that region granting enjoyment and liberation.
In that excellent region is a linga called Bhaskareshvara; those who, having bathed in the pool, see that god Maheshvara,
the three-eyed god of gods worshipped long ago by the Sun, freed from all sins and mounted on excellent celestial cars,
sung to by Gandharvas, go to Shiva's world; they stay there joyfully for a whole kalpa, O best of brahmins.
Having enjoyed abundant charming pleasures in Shiva's world, when their merit is exhausted they come here and are born in an excellent family,
or in the house of yogins, masters of the Vedas and their limbs; they are born as excellent brahmins devoted to the welfare of all beings,
skilled in the meaning of the scriptures of liberation, even-minded everywhere; having attained the excellent yoga of Shambhu, they then go to liberation.
In that holy, excellent region, O brahmins, whatever linga is seen, whether it is worshipped or not, anywhere — in a forest or amid streets,
at a crossroads or in a cremation ground, wherever it stands — seeing that linga, calm and composed with faith,
bathing it with devotion and worshipping it with charming perfumes and flowers, with incense, lamps, food offerings, salutations and hymns,
with prostrations like a staff, and with dance, song and the like — having worshipped thus by rule, a man goes to Shiva's world.
Or a woman, O tigers among brahmins, who worships with faith obtains the fruit told before; there is no need for deliberation.
Who, O best of sages, can tell all the virtues of that excellent region, except the god Maheshvara?
Going to that best of regions, with faith or even without faith, in the months beginning with Madhava, whether man or woman,
on whatever day, O brahmins, having bathed in the water of Bindusaras, whoever sees the god Virupaksha and the boon-giving Goddess Shiva,
the Gana Chanda, Karttikeya, Ganesha, the bull, the wish-fulfilling tree and Savitri, goes to Shiva's world.
Having bathed duly in the Kapila holy place, destroyer of sin, one obtains one's desired wishes and goes to Shiva's world.
Whoever, with senses controlled, duly performs the stambhya rite there raises twenty-one generations of his family and goes to Shiva's world.
In the auspicious Shiva-region of Ekamraka, equal to Varanasi, whoever bathes there surely obtains liberation.
The wise man with senses controlled, going to these holy places in Viraja and to the Ashtatirtha, bathing duly and bowing to the gods,
freed from all sins, mounted on an excellent celestial car and sung to by Gandharvas, is honoured in my world.
Whoever offers rice-balls in my region Viraja brings imperishable satisfaction to the ancestors; there is no doubt.
Those men who give up their bodies in my region Viraja, O best of sages, attain liberation.
The mortal who bathes in the ocean, sees Kapila Hari and sees the goddess Varahi goes to the abode of the gods.
There are other holy places and sacred shrines too, O best of sages; they should be learned at the proper time.
On the northern shore of the ocean, in that land, O best of brahmins, is a supremely secret region that grants liberation and destroys sin,
strewn everywhere with sand, pure, granting all desires, ten yojanas in extent — a region most rare,
with ashokas, arjunas, punnagas, bakulas, sarala trees, jackfruits, coconuts, shalas, palmyras and kapitthakas,
champakas, karnikaras, mangoes, bilvas and patalas, kadambas, kovidaras, lakuchas and nagakesaras,
prachina-amalakas, lodhras, oranges, dhavas and khadiras, sarjas, bhurjas, ashvakarnas, tamalas and devadarus,
mandaras, parijatas, banyans, aloe and sandal, date palms, amratakas, siddhas, muchukundas and kimshukas,
ashvatthas, saptaparnas, madhudharas and shubhanjanas, shimshapas, amalakas, nipas, nimbas, tindus and vibhitakas,
rich in the fruits and fragrances of every season, bright with the flowers of every season, delighting the mind, fair, resounding with various birds,
with sounds from the mouths of birds, pleasant to the ear, very sweet, intoxicating in strength, giving joy to the mind,
with chakoras, shatapatras, bhringarajas, parrots, cuckoos, sparrows, haritas and jivajivakas,
priyaputras, chatakas and others with sweet voices, pleasant to the ear and dear, singing in their lovely haunts,
with groves of ketaki, atimuktas and kubjakas, malati, kunda and bana flowers, and red and white karaviras,
jambira, karuna and ankola, pomegranates, citrons, matulungas, areca palms, hintalas and plantain groves,
and other various trees, other charming flowers, canopies of creepers and shrubs, and various reservoirs,
long ponds, tanks, lotus pools and step-wells, various holy reservoirs adorned with clusters of lotuses,
and charming lakes with clear water, covered all around with water-lilies, white lotuses and lovely blue lotuses,
with kahlaras and lotuses too; with kadambas, chakravakas and water-fowl,
karandavas, plavas, swans, tortoises, fish and cormorants, crowded with gallinules and cranes and beautiful with koyashti herons,
with these and other water-creatures calling all around, with birds and aquatic creatures and flowers born in water.
Thus with various trees and flowers born on land and in water, with celibate students, householders, forest-dwellers and mendicants,
adorned with the classes devoted to their own dharma and with others, crowded with happy, well-fed people, full of men and women,
the abode of all knowledge, the mine of all dharma and virtue — thus endowed with every good quality is that most rare region.
There dwells, O best of sages, the renowned Purushottama; as far as the boundary of Utkala extends, as declared in the order of the directions,
so far, by the grace of Krishna, is that land most holy, the land where Purushottama, the soul of the universe, abides.
Jagannatha, pervading the world — there everything is established. I, Rudra, Shakra and the gods led by Agni
always dwell in that land, O best of sages; all the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the ancestors, gods and men,
Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas, sages of strict vows, the Valakhilya seers, and the lords of creatures led by Kashyapa,
Suparnas, Kinnaras, Nagas and other heaven-dwellers, the four Vedas with their limbs and various scriptures,
the Itihasas and Puranas, sacrifices with excellent fees, various holy rivers, holy places and shrines,
the oceans and the mountains — all are established in that land. In so holy a land, served by gods, sages and ancestors,
endowed with every enjoyment, who would not like to dwell? What land is superior, and what could be greater than that,
where the god Purushottama himself, the giver of liberation, dwells? Blessed are those men, like gods, who dwell in Utkala,
who bathe in the water of the king of holy places and see Purushottama; those mortals dwell in heaven and do not go to Yama's abode.
Those who dwell in the holy region of Utkala at Shri Purushottama — fruitful is the life of those wise people of Utkala,
who see the best of gods, with gracious long eyes, lovely brows, hair and crown, lovely ear-ornaments,
a lovely smile, lovely teeth, adorned with lovely earrings, with a fine nose, fine cheeks, fine forehead and fine marks —
the lotus face of Krishna, which gives joy to the three worlds.
How did that tiger among kings fashion Krishna, Rama and Subhadra, O lord of creatures, and how did he protect the region?
How did the wise king install Krishna and the others, worshipped by the gods, in that palace, the best in the world?
All this, O best of gods, you should tell in detail, just as it happened — the whole story of that wise one.
We are never satisfied with the nectar of your words; we wish to hear, O Brahman, for our curiosity is great.

Well done, well done, O best of brahmins, that you ask about this ancient account, which removes all sins, is holy, grants enjoyment and liberation, and is auspicious.
